summary: This experimental document describes a process in which Internet-Draft authors record the status of known implementations in an Implementation Status section. This helps reviewers and working groups give due weight to documents backed by running code. It was replaced by RFC 7942.

plainLanguage.summary: Authors add a section saying who has built their idea so far, so reviewers know it really works. A newer document replaced this one.

questions: implementation status section in internet drafts
how do working groups use implementation information
subtitle: Documenting implementations to improve protocol standards

tldr.problem: IETF protocols are published as RFCs even if no one has built them yet, making it hard for reviewers to know if a specification is clear or correct.
tldr.mechanism: Draft specifications can include an Implementation Status section that lists all known implementations, their maturity, coverage, and lessons learned, giving reviewers evidence that the protocol actually works.
tldr.outcome: This transparency encourages implementers to build early, helps working groups make better decisions, and lets protocol authors fix problems before standards become permanent. It was replaced by RFC 7942.

today: RFC 6982 is an Experimental specification and has been replaced by RFC 7942, which recommends the Implementation Status section as a standard practice for Internet-Drafts. The practice of documenting implementations in protocol drafts continues to help reviewers evaluate running code and accelerate improvement in IETF standards.

sections.title: Why Running Code Matters
sections.content:
The IETF motto is rough consensus and running code, but implementation is not a requirement for an RFC. Many protocols are published without anyone having built them. This creates a risk: the specification might be unclear, impractical, or contain errors that only show up when someone tries to code it.

Some IETF areas have historically required implementations before publication (such as the Routing Area), but most do not. This document proposes a simple way to record which protocols have implementations, so reviewers and working groups can decide how much weight to give running code when comparing competing proposals.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules that nobody has tested often have hidden problems. By saying who has tested the rule in real code, reviewers can better judge if it is good.

sections.title: The Implementation Status Section
sections.content:
Authors can add an Implementation Status section to an Internet-Draft. This section, placed before Security Considerations, lists each known implementation and describes:

  • The organization responsible for it.
  • The implementation's name and a link to its web page or source code.
  • A brief description of what it does.
  • Its maturity level: research, prototype, alpha, beta, production, widely used, etc.
  • Coverage: which parts of the spec are implemented and which versions were implemented.
  • Licensing: proprietary, open source, free to use with conditions, etc.
  • Implementation experience: lessons learned, compatibility issues, or missing features.
  • Contact information: email or web link for questions.

The section can also include interoperability reports between implementations. Working group chairs must ensure the section is not used as marketing material.

This information is time-dependent and inappropriate for a published RFC, so the authors should request that the section be removed before publication.
sections.plainLanguage: Authors list what groups have built their protocol, how complete it is, and what they learned. It helps reviewers understand whether the idea actually works.

sections.title: Why This Helps
sections.content:
Documenting implementations provides several benefits to the IETF process:

  • Working groups can prioritize competing proposals based on evidence of running code.
  • Reviewers and ADs can decide whether to move a draft to a different standards track.
  • Knowing that people must disclose their work motivates early implementation and experimentation.
  • Other participants can study the code to check if the specification matches the implementation, and whether the spec is missing details.
  • Interoperability testing becomes easier when implementers know about each other.
  • Open source projects let people learn the protocol by reading real code.
  • The mere existence of an implementation proves that difficult-to-understand features are actually buildable.
sections.plainLanguage: When authors know their code will be shown to reviewers, they implement earlier, find problems sooner, and let others test whether everything works together.

sections.title: Running as an Experiment
sections.content:
The RFC presents this as an experiment, voluntary and open-ended. The authors do not claim that implementation is now required, nor that running code must be given preference over other considerations. Instead, they encourage I-D authors to try including Implementation Status sections, and working group chairs to mention this practice to their document editors.

The experiment was planned to last 18 months from publication, with the authors to report on adoption and usefulness. The scope covers all IETF Internet-Drafts with implementable specifications in working groups and on the Independent Stream, but not RFCs themselves.

After the initial experiment period, I-D authors remain free to include Implementation Status sections even if the experiment formally concludes.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF is trying this idea to see if it helps. If it works well, it can become a regular part of the standards process.

sections.title: Where This Stands Now
sections.content: RFC 6982 is an Experimental specification and was replaced by RFC 7942, which made the Implementation Status section a recommended practice for Internet-Drafts. The concept proved valuable: tracking implementations early in the standards process helps identify practical issues and gives reviewers better information about the maturity and real-world applicability of proposed protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: This experiment worked well, so a newer document made it a standard practice for drafts.
